questions.question: What is the PRIMARY problem that HashiCorp Vault solves?
options: Slow database queries in distributed systems
Secrets sprawl — credentials hardcoded in config files, code, and environment variables
Lack of network encryption between microservices
Insufficient container orchestration capabilities
questions.explanation: Vault solves secrets sprawl: credentials scattered in config files, environment variables, wikis, and code repositories. It centralizes secrets with audit logging, dynamic secrets, fine-grained access control, automatic rotation, and encryption as a service.

questions.question: Which Vault secrets engine generates real AWS IAM credentials with a configurable TTL that are automatically revoked on expiry?
options: KV v2 secrets engine
Transit secrets engine
AWS secrets engine (dynamic credentials)
Cubbyhole secrets engine
questions.explanation: The AWS secrets engine generates dynamic IAM access keys on demand with a TTL. Vault creates the IAM credentials, hands them to the application, and automatically deletes them when the lease expires. Each application gets unique credentials — no shared long-lived keys.

questions.question: An application needs to authenticate to Vault without human interaction. Which auth method is specifically designed for machine-to-Vault authentication?
options: LDAP auth method
GitHub auth method
AppRole auth method
Userpass auth method
questions.explanation: AppRole is designed for automated pipelines and applications. It uses a role_id (non-sensitive, can be embedded in the app) and a secret_id (sensitive, delivered separately at deploy time). This separation enforces security even in automated environments.

questions.question: What is the fundamental identity object returned by ALL Vault auth methods after successful authentication?
options: An API key
A Vault token
A session cookie
An X.509 certificate
questions.explanation: All Vault auth methods (AppRole, LDAP, Kubernetes, AWS, etc.) return a Vault token after successful authentication. The token has attached policies, a TTL, and an accessor. It is the core identity mechanism used for all subsequent API calls.

questions.question: What are the capabilities that a Vault policy can grant on a path? (select the complete list)
options: read, write, execute, delete
create, read, update, delete, list, sudo, deny
get, put, post, patch, delete
allow, deny, log, forward
questions.explanation: Vault policy capabilities: create (write new), read, update (overwrite existing), delete, list (enumerate keys), sudo (root-restricted operations), deny (explicit deny overrides any allow). Policies are written in HCL or JSON and assigned to tokens at authentication time.

questions.question: What is the KEY difference between KV v1 and KV v2 secrets engines?
options: KV v2 supports encryption; v1 does not
KV v1 supports versioning; v2 does not
KV v2 maintains versioned history and supports soft-delete; v1 overwrites data with no recovery
KV v1 supports dynamic secrets; v2 is static only
questions.explanation: KV v2 is versioned: writing a new value keeps the old versions (configurable max). Soft-delete marks a version deleted but allows recovery. Destroy permanently removes a version. KV v1 silently overwrites data with no way to recover previous values. Use KV v2 for production.

questions.question: What is a 'dynamic secret' in Vault and what is the main advantage over static secrets?
options: A secret stored in an encrypted file — advantage is disk encryption
A secret generated on-demand with a TTL that is automatically revoked — each request gets unique credentials, no shared long-lived secrets
A secret that rotates on a fixed schedule — advantage is predictability
A secret that expires after first use — advantage is one-time access
questions.explanation: Dynamic secrets are generated on-demand (real database users, AWS IAM keys) with a TTL. They auto-revoke when the lease expires. Key advantages: short-lived (reduces exposure window), unique per application (breach isolation), no manual rotation needed. The AWS and Database secrets engines are primary examples.

questions.question: A Vault lease is about to expire. The application calls vault lease renew. What happens if the renewal would exceed the secret's max_lease_ttl?
options: Vault allows the renewal and silently extends max_lease_ttl
Vault grants a renewal up to the max_lease_ttl ceiling, then the secret must be re-requested
Vault revokes the secret immediately
Vault converts the lease to a non-expiring permanent secret
questions.explanation: max_lease_ttl is a hard ceiling. Vault will renew the lease but only up to the max_lease_ttl — it cannot be renewed beyond it. Once max_lease_ttl is reached, the application must request a new secret (which creates new credentials). This design prevents indefinitely long-lived secrets.

questions.question: In AppRole authentication, which component is considered NON-sensitive and can be safely embedded in application code or configuration?
options: The secret_id
The role_id
The Vault token
The wrapped response token
questions.explanation: The role_id is analogous to a username — it identifies the role but doesn't grant access by itself. It can be embedded in application config. The secret_id is sensitive (like a password) and must be delivered separately, ideally at deploy time via response wrapping or a secure channel.

questions.question: An application needs to encrypt sensitive data before storing it in a database but should NOT store the encryption keys itself. Which Vault secrets engine solves this?
options: KV v2 secrets engine
Database secrets engine
Transit secrets engine (encryption-as-a-service)
PKI secrets engine
questions.explanation: The Transit secrets engine provides encryption-as-a-service. The application sends plaintext to Vault, receives ciphertext back. Vault manages the encryption keys and never exposes them. The application stores only ciphertext. Key rotation is supported — Vault can rewrap existing ciphertext with a newer key version.

questions.question: A company wants to eliminate long-lived TLS certificates (valid 1-2 years). Which Vault secrets engine enables issuing short-lived certificates on demand?
options: SSH secrets engine
PKI secrets engine
Transit secrets engine
KV v2 secrets engine
questions.explanation: The PKI secrets engine acts as an internal Certificate Authority. It issues X.509 certificates with configurable TTLs — from hours to days instead of years. Services request certificates at startup, certificates expire naturally. This eliminates manual certificate rotation and reduces the blast radius of compromised certificates.

questions.question: A developer runs vault read database/creds/my-role and gets a username and password. What happens to those credentials when the Vault lease expires?
options: The credentials remain valid indefinitely — Vault only tracks them internally
Vault sends a notification to the application to stop using them
Vault connects to the database and drops the created user, revoking access
The credentials are archived in the KV store
questions.explanation: The Database secrets engine creates real database users with the granted TTL. When the lease expires (or is explicitly revoked), Vault uses its stored connection credentials to connect to the database and execute the DROP USER statement. This makes revocation automatic and immediate.

questions.question: Which Vault component runs as a client-side daemon, handles automatic authentication, and writes secrets to local files for applications to consume?
options: Vault Server
Vault Agent
Vault Proxy
Vault Sentinel
questions.explanation: Vault Agent is a client daemon that handles auto-auth (AppRole, Kubernetes, AWS), automatically renews tokens and leases, and uses template rendering to write secrets to config files. Applications can read secrets from files without needing the Vault SDK, and Vault Agent handles all TTL management.

questions.question: A team uses response wrapping to deliver an AppRole secret_id to a new service. When the service goes to unwrap the token, it gets an error saying the token has already been used. What does this indicate?
options: The wrapping token expired due to clock skew
Someone intercepted and unwrapped the token before the intended recipient
The Vault server restarted and cleared wrapping tokens
The service used the wrong Vault address
questions.explanation: Response wrapping creates a single-use token. If the intended recipient gets an error that the wrapping token was already used, it means someone else (an interceptor) already unwrapped it. This is a key security feature: tampering becomes detectable. The team should investigate the delivery pipeline and revoke any secrets that may have been exposed.

questions.question: What happens to all Vault operations if ALL configured audit devices fail to write their logs?
options: Vault continues normally and queues audit logs for later
Vault switches to a degraded mode with reduced logging
Vault blocks ALL requests until at least one audit device is operational
Vault sends audit logs to a fallback syslog endpoint
questions.explanation: Vault prioritizes audit integrity over availability. If all enabled audit devices fail to write, Vault blocks all operations. This is by design — it prevents operating in an unaudited state. For HA environments, configure multiple audit devices (file + syslog) so a single failure doesn't halt operations.

questions.question: A Vault server starts and is in 'sealed' state. What must happen before it can serve any requests?
options: The server must be registered with the license server
Sufficient unseal key shares must be provided to reconstruct the master key
The admin must restart the Vault service with a special flag
The root token must be re-created using vault operator init
questions.explanation: Vault uses Shamir's Secret Sharing to split the master key. Unsealing requires providing enough key shares (quorum) to reconstruct the master key and decrypt Vault's storage. By default: 5 key shares with threshold 3. Auto-unseal (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault) automates this for production HA deployments.

questions.question: In a Vault HA cluster, a client sends a request to a standby node. What does the standby node do?
options: Rejects the request with a 503 error
Processes the request locally using its cached state
Forwards the request to the active node transparently
Promotes itself to active and processes the request
questions.explanation: In Vault HA, only one node is active at a time. Standby nodes forward requests to the active node transparently. From the client's perspective, the request succeeds regardless of which node it hits. When the active node fails, a standby is promoted to active (typically within seconds).

questions.question: What is the main advantage of Vault Raft integrated storage compared to using a Consul storage backend?
options: Raft provides better encryption for stored secrets
Raft eliminates the need for an external storage dependency — Vault manages its own cluster storage
Raft supports more concurrent connections than Consul
Raft allows larger secrets to be stored
questions.explanation: Vault Raft integrated storage (introduced in Vault 1.4) eliminates the need for Consul or another external storage backend. Vault manages its own consensus and replication using the Raft algorithm. This simplifies deployment, reduces operational overhead, and is the recommended storage backend for new Vault deployments.

questions.question: A user authenticates to Vault via LDAP and also via GitHub. How does Vault's identity system track this as the same person?
options: Vault cannot correlate logins across different auth methods
An Entity is created with Aliases for each auth method — both logins resolve to the same entity and policies
The user must manually link their accounts in the Vault UI
Only the most recently used auth method is active at a time
questions.explanation: Vault Identity creates an Entity that represents a unique user or service. Each auth method login that matches creates an Alias linked to that entity. Both the LDAP alias and GitHub alias resolve to the same entity, so policies assigned to the entity apply regardless of which auth method was used.

questions.question: Vault Namespaces is a feature that allows multi-tenant deployments within a single cluster. Which Vault edition includes Namespaces?
options: Vault OSS (open-source)
Vault Community Edition
Vault Enterprise only
All Vault editions including the free tier
questions.explanation: Vault Namespaces is an Enterprise-only feature. It creates fully isolated Vault environments within a single cluster — each namespace has its own auth methods, secrets engines, policies, and tokens. This enables Vault-as-a-Service use cases where teams manage their own isolated Vault namespace.

questions.question: A Kubernetes pod needs to authenticate to Vault without any pre-provisioned credentials. Which authentication mechanism allows this?
options: AppRole with the role_id stored in a Kubernetes Secret
Kubernetes auth method using the pod's automatically mounted ServiceAccount JWT
TLS certificate auth using the pod's TLS cert
AWS IAM auth using the node's instance profile
questions.explanation: The Kubernetes auth method validates the pod's ServiceAccount JWT token (mounted at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token) with the Kubernetes TokenReview API. No pre-provisioned credentials are needed — the pod's identity is proven by Kubernetes itself. Vault binds roles to specific ServiceAccount names and namespaces.

questions.question: What path prefix does Vault use for ALL auth method configuration?
options: vault/auth/
auth/
sys/auth/
login/
questions.explanation: Auth methods are mounted under the auth/ path prefix. For example: auth/approle/, auth/kubernetes/, auth/ldap/. The sys/ path prefix is for Vault system operations (mounting, sealing, audit, policy management). Secrets engines are mounted at their configured paths (e.g., secret/, aws/, database/).

questions.question: A high-throughput application creates thousands of Vault tokens per second. Which token type is optimized for this scenario and why?
options: Service tokens — they're more secure for high-volume workloads
Batch tokens — they're lightweight, not stored in Vault, and faster to create
Root tokens — they bypass storage overhead
Orphan tokens — they don't need parent token management
questions.explanation: Batch tokens are encoded entirely in the token string and not stored in Vault's storage backend. This makes them extremely lightweight — no storage write per token creation. They cannot be renewed and have no children, but for short-lived, high-volume use cases (Lambda functions, CI/CD jobs) they are far more efficient than service tokens.

questions.question: Which Vault secrets engine is automatically mounted, scoped exclusively to the current token, and used internally for response wrapping?
options: KV v1 engine at secret/
Identity secrets engine
Cubbyhole secrets engine
System secrets engine at sys/
questions.explanation: The Cubbyhole secrets engine is always mounted at cubbyhole/ and is private to each token — no other token can access another token's cubbyhole. Response wrapping stores the wrapped secret in the cubbyhole of a single-use wrapping token. When the wrapping token expires, its cubbyhole (and the wrapped secret) is also destroyed.

questions.question: An operator needs to revoke a specific token without knowing the token's actual value. Which Vault concept allows this?
options: Token alias
Token accessor
Token entity ID
Token display name
questions.explanation: Every Vault token has an accessor — an opaque reference that allows administrative operations (lookup, revoke) without needing the token itself. Audit logs store the accessor, not the token. An operator can run vault token revoke -accessor <accessor> to revoke a specific token identified from audit logs.

questions.question: A Vault policy contains path 'secret/data/app/*' { capabilities = ['read'] }. Which operation would this policy DENY?
options: vault kv get secret/app/config
vault kv get secret/app/database/password
vault kv put secret/app/config api_key=new
vault kv list secret/app/
questions.explanation: The policy grants only 'read' capability on the path. Writing (vault kv put) requires 'create' or 'update' capability. Listing requires 'list' capability on the parent path. The policy explicitly restricts writes, so vault kv put would be denied. Note: list also requires listing the path secret/metadata/app/ for KV v2.

questions.question: What does 'vault operator init' do and when is it run?
options: It starts the Vault server process
It initializes a new Vault cluster, generating unseal keys and a root token — run ONCE on a brand new cluster
It resets an existing cluster to factory defaults
It registers the Vault server with HashiCorp's licensing servers
questions.explanation: vault operator init is run exactly once on a new Vault cluster. It generates the Shamir key shares (unseal keys) and an initial root token. The unseal keys must be securely distributed to key holders immediately. The root token should be used minimally to bootstrap initial configuration, then revoked.

questions.question: A team wants to create a Vault policy that allows listing secrets in secret/team-a/ but prevents reading the secret VALUES. Which capability achieves this?
options: Create capability on secret/team-a/
List capability on the metadata path without read on the data path
Read capability with a condition blocking value access
Sudo capability with read disabled
questions.explanation: In KV v2, listing secrets requires 'list' on 'secret/metadata/team-a/*'. Reading secret values requires 'read' on 'secret/data/team-a/*'. By granting list on the metadata path only (without read on data), users can see secret names but cannot read their values. This separation is a KV v2 advantage over v1.

questions.question: Which Vault auto-unseal mechanism uses a cloud Key Management Service (KMS) to automatically unseal Vault on startup?
options: Shamir auto-unseal: stores key shares in a file
Cloud KMS auto-unseal: AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, GCP Cloud KMS wrap the master key
Transit auto-unseal: uses another Vault's transit engine
HSM auto-unseal only (no cloud options available)
questions.explanation: Auto-unseal uses a cloud KMS (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, GCP Cloud KMS) or HSM to wrap/unwrap the Vault master key. On startup, Vault calls the KMS to decrypt the master key automatically — no human key holders needed. This is the recommended approach for HA production deployments. Transit auto-unseal (using another Vault's Transit engine) is also a valid option.

questions.question: What happens when vault lease revoke is called on a dynamic database secret?
options: The lease record is deleted from Vault but the database user remains
Vault marks the secret as revoked but waits for the TTL to expire before acting
Vault immediately connects to the database and drops the created user
The application is notified via webhook to stop using the credentials
questions.explanation: Revoking a dynamic database secret lease triggers immediate revocation: Vault uses its stored database connection to DROP the user that was created for that lease. The credentials become invalid instantly, not after the TTL expires. This is valuable for incident response when a credential may have been compromised.

questions.question: A Vault token has a TTL of 1 hour but the application needs it to remain valid for 8 hours. The token's max_ttl is 24 hours. What should the application do?
options: Create a new token by re-authenticating after each hour
Call vault token renew before the TTL expires to extend it (up to max_ttl)
Change the token's TTL using vault token update
Enable token immortality by setting TTL to 0
questions.explanation: Vault tokens with 'renewable: true' can be renewed before expiry using vault token renew (or the API equivalent). Each renewal extends the TTL by its increment, but the token cannot be renewed past max_ttl. Vault Agent automates this for applications. Setting TTL to 0 does NOT make a token immortal — it uses the system default TTL.

questions.question: Which Vault secrets engine should be used to generate one-time passwords (OTP) for SSH access to servers?
options: KV v2 secrets engine with SSH key storage
PKI secrets engine with SSH certificates
SSH secrets engine in OTP mode or CA mode
Transit secrets engine with RSA keys
questions.explanation: The SSH secrets engine has two modes: OTP mode generates a single-use password for a specific user/host, and CA mode signs SSH public keys creating short-lived SSH certificates. Both eliminate the need to distribute and manage SSH keys manually. CA mode is preferred for scale as it doesn't require a Vault helper on each target host.

questions.question: What does the 'default' policy in Vault contain and when is it applied?
options: Full administrative access — applied to admin users only
A minimal set of self-service permissions (token renewal, self-lookup) — attached to ALL tokens automatically
No permissions — it's a placeholder policy with empty rules
Read-only access to all secret paths
questions.explanation: The 'default' policy is automatically attached to every token created in Vault. It grants minimal permissions like token renewal (auth/token/renew-self), self-lookup (auth/token/lookup-self), and revocation (auth/token/revoke-self). You can add more permissions to the default policy or explicitly exclude it using token_no_default_policy in auth roles.

questions.question: A Vault transit key has been rotated (now on version 3). Data was encrypted with versions 1 and 2. How does Vault handle decryption of old ciphertext?
options: Old ciphertext can no longer be decrypted after key rotation
Vault maintains all key versions and can decrypt ciphertext from any non-deleted version
Vault automatically re-encrypts all stored data with the new key on rotation
The application must manually specify the key version when decrypting
questions.explanation: Transit keys maintain all historical versions. The ciphertext format includes the key version prefix (vault:v1:..., vault:v2:...). Vault uses the correct version to decrypt. Key rotation creates a new version for new encryptions; old versions remain for decryption. Use vault write transit/keys/mykey/trim min_decryption_version=2 to remove older versions.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'vault operator raft snapshot save' command?
options: Creates a backup of only the Vault configuration files
Creates a point-in-time snapshot of the entire Raft storage backend for disaster recovery
Exports all secret values to an encrypted file
Captures the current unseal key shares for secure storage
questions.explanation: vault operator raft snapshot save creates a binary snapshot of the entire Raft storage state. This snapshot can be restored with vault operator raft snapshot restore to recover from data loss or cluster failure. It captures all Vault data: secrets, policies, auth config, and audit logs. Regular automated snapshots are a critical backup practice.

questions.question: An AppRole role is configured with secret_id_num_uses=1. What happens when a CI/CD system tries to use the same secret_id a second time?
options: Vault grants the authentication but logs a warning
Vault authenticates successfully but reduces the remaining use count to -1
Vault rejects the authentication — the secret_id is consumed after first use
Vault refreshes the secret_id automatically with a new one
questions.explanation: Setting secret_id_num_uses=1 makes the secret_id a single-use credential — after one successful authentication, it's consumed and cannot be used again. This is the recommended setting for CI/CD pipelines where each deployment should receive and consume a fresh secret_id. It prevents credential reuse if a secret_id is leaked.

questions.question: What is the vault.hcl (or vault.json) configuration file used for?
options: Storing secret values that Vault reads at startup
Defining the Vault server's storage backend, listener, cluster address, and seal configuration
Defining policies that are loaded automatically on first startup
Storing the root token for disaster recovery
questions.explanation: vault.hcl configures the Vault server process: storage backend (raft, consul, dynamodb), listener (TCP address, TLS certificates), cluster_addr (for HA), api_addr, seal configuration (for auto-unseal), and telemetry. It does NOT store secrets or policies — those are managed via the API/CLI after the server starts.

questions.question: Which Vault path stores Vault's own system configuration, health status, and mount management endpoints?
options: admin/
vault/
sys/
config/
questions.explanation: The sys/ path is Vault's system API. Key endpoints: sys/health (cluster health), sys/seal (seal the vault), sys/unseal (unseal), sys/mounts (manage secrets engine mounts), sys/auth (manage auth method mounts), sys/policies (manage policies), sys/audit (manage audit devices). Access to sys/ paths typically requires sudo capability.

questions.question: A Vault admin wants to provide an external team temporary read access to a specific secret, with the access token self-destructing after delivery. Which mechanism achieves this?
options: Create an IAM user for the team with read-only access
Share the root token temporarily
Use response wrapping — deliver a wrapping token that can only be unwrapped once
Enable public access on the secret path temporarily
questions.explanation: Response wrapping creates a single-use wrapping token that contains the secret. The admin delivers the wrapping token to the team. When unwrapped, the actual secret is returned and the wrapping token is consumed. If someone intercepts and unwraps it first, the team gets an error — making interception detectable. The wrapping token also has a TTL, after which it expires.

questions.question: What is the 'orphan' flag on a Vault token?
options: A token that has no attached policies
A token whose parent has expired — it survives independently of the creating token's lifecycle
A token that cannot create child tokens
A token created without a TTL
questions.explanation: Normally, revoking a parent token revokes all its child tokens. An orphan token (token_type = orphan) has no parent — it exists independently. This is important for long-running services that authenticate via AppRole: the AppRole login token is ephemeral (parent), but the service shouldn't lose access just because the login token expired. Orphan tokens persist until their own TTL expires or they're explicitly revoked.

questions.question: A Vault audit log shows a request with HMAC-ed token value. Why are token values HMACed in audit logs?
options: To compress the logs for storage efficiency
To prevent the actual token from being readable in logs — protecting against log-based token theft while still allowing correlation
To encrypt all audit log entries for compliance
To allow log replay for debugging purposes
questions.explanation: Vault HMACs sensitive values (tokens, secrets) in audit logs using a salt. The HMAC allows correlation (same token = same HMAC across all log entries) without exposing the actual token value. An attacker who obtains audit logs cannot extract usable tokens. Administrators use accessors (not HMACs) for operational token management.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'vault kv delete' and 'vault kv destroy' in KV v2?
options: delete removes the secret entirely; destroy just marks it inactive
delete is a soft-delete (versions marked deleted but recoverable); destroy permanently removes specific version data
Both are identical operations
destroy removes all versions; delete removes only the latest
questions.explanation: KV v2 soft-delete (vault kv delete): marks the version as deleted, but the data remains recoverable with vault kv undelete. Destroy (vault kv destroy): permanently removes the version data — irreversible. The metadata (version history) still shows the version existed, but the secret data is gone. Use destroy for secrets that must be truly purged (e.g., compromised credentials).

questions.question: An application runs in AWS EC2. Which Vault auth method allows the EC2 instance to authenticate without any pre-placed secrets?
options: AppRole with the role_id stored in user-data
AWS auth method using the EC2 instance identity document signed by AWS
TLS certificate auth using the instance's TLS certificate
LDAP auth using the EC2 hostname
questions.explanation: The AWS auth method supports EC2 authentication using the signed instance identity document (from IMDS). Vault verifies the document's signature with AWS's public certificate, confirming the identity of the EC2 instance without pre-placed credentials. Vault can bind roles to specific AMI IDs, accounts, regions, or IAM roles.

questions.question: What does 'vault operator step-down' do in a Vault HA cluster?
options: Shuts down the entire Vault cluster
Forces the active node to relinquish leadership, triggering a failover to a standby node
Removes a node from the cluster permanently
Rotates the cluster's internal encryption keys
questions.explanation: vault operator step-down forces the active Vault node to give up its leadership. A standby node then wins the leader election and becomes active. This is used for planned maintenance, rolling upgrades, or testing failover. The stepped-down node becomes a standby and remains in the cluster.

questions.question: Which Vault feature allows path-based routing rules to override or deny access based on contextual information like time of day or IP address? (Enterprise)
options: ACL templating in policies
Vault Sentinel / Endpoint Governing Policies (EGPs) and Role Governing Policies (RGPs)
LDAP group-based policy assignment
Token metadata conditions
questions.explanation: Vault Enterprise includes Sentinel-based Endpoint Governing Policies (EGPs) and Role Governing Policies (RGPs). These allow complex policy logic (time-based, IP-based, MFA-required conditions) using HashiCorp Sentinel's policy-as-code framework. This goes beyond static ACL capabilities. EGPs apply to specific paths; RGPs apply to roles.

questions.question: A team stores secrets at secret/data/team-a/db. They want to enforce that only tokens with entity metadata 'team=team-a' can access this path. Which Vault ACL template feature enables this?
options: Vault cannot use token metadata for policy decisions
ACL templating with {{identity.entity.metadata.team}} in the policy path
LDAP group binding to the secret path
AWS IAM condition keys in Vault policies
questions.explanation: Vault ACL templating allows dynamic policy paths using identity metadata. A policy like path 'secret/data/{{identity.entity.metadata.team}}/*' { capabilities = ['read'] } restricts each entity to only their team's secrets path. The placeholder resolves at policy evaluation time based on the authenticated entity's metadata.

questions.question: What is the FIRST step before enabling and configuring a secrets engine mount in Vault?
options: Create a policy granting access to the mount path
Enable the secrets engine at a path using vault secrets enable
Write the configuration to the config/ path
Restart the Vault server to load the engine plugin
questions.explanation: The first step is vault secrets enable -path=myengine <engine-type> (e.g., vault secrets enable -path=aws aws). This mounts the engine at the specified path. After mounting, you configure the engine (e.g., vault write aws/config/root credentials). Policies can be created before or after, but the engine must be mounted before it can be used.

questions.question: An operator runs vault token lookup and sees 'renewable: false'. What does this mean for the token lifecycle?
options: The token will never expire
The token can only be renewed by root users
The token will expire at its TTL and cannot be extended — a new token must be obtained
The token can be renewed but the TTL won't increase
questions.explanation: A non-renewable token cannot be extended with vault token renew. Once its TTL expires, it becomes invalid. The application must re-authenticate to get a new token. Batch tokens are always non-renewable by design. Some auth method roles can be configured to issue non-renewable tokens for security purposes.

questions.question: What is the vault CLI environment variable used to set the Vault server address so you don't have to pass -address on every command?
options: VAULT_URL
VAULT_HOST
VAULT_ADDR
VAULT_ENDPOINT
questions.explanation: VAULT_ADDR sets the default Vault server address (e.g., export VAULT_ADDR=https://vault.example.com:8200). Other important Vault environment variables: VAULT_TOKEN (default token), VAULT_NAMESPACE (namespace for Enterprise), VAULT_CACERT (CA certificate path), VAULT_TLS_SKIP_VERIFY (skip TLS verification, NOT for production).

questions.question: A company wants to ensure that even if the Vault database is stolen, stored secrets cannot be read. What protects the data at rest in Vault's storage backend?
options: The storage backend's native encryption (e.g., S3 SSE)
Vault's barrier encryption — all data written to storage is encrypted using the master key before being stored
TLS encryption on the Vault API listener
File system permissions on the storage directory
questions.explanation: Vault's cryptographic barrier encrypts ALL data before writing to the storage backend using the master key (derived from the unseal keys). This means even if someone steals the raw storage (Consul KV, DynamoDB, Raft files), they cannot read any secrets without the master key. This is why Vault starts 'sealed' — the master key is not in memory until unsealing occurs.
